**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

questions.enonce_markdown: How pivotal was the role of Samuel as a king maker in Israel? (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Samuel was the last of the judges, a priest and a prophet. At the end of the period of the judges, the elders asked him for a king (1 Samuel 8). He then anointed Saul and later David. His part was therefore central, although the narrative also stresses that God was the true initiator.

**1. Samuel's part in the beginning of the monarchy.**
- *Hearing the demand.* The elders said that Samuel was old, his sons did not follow his ways, and they wanted a king "like all the nations". Samuel was displeased but prayed. God told him to listen and said that the people had rejected Him as king.
- *The warning.* He described how a king would take sons for war, daughters for service and a share of the land and produce (1 Samuel 8).
- *Choosing and anointing Saul.* Led by God, Samuel received Saul, anointed him privately (1 Samuel 9 and 10) and, at Mizpah, presented him to the people by lot. After Saul's victory at Jabesh-gilead, Samuel renewed the kingship at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11).
- *Farewell address.* Samuel reminded the people that king and people must obey the Lord and warned them of the consequences of disobedience (1 Samuel 12).
- *Rejecting Saul and anointing David.* When Saul disobeyed, Samuel told him that the kingdom would be taken from him (1 Samuel 13 and 15), and he later anointed David at Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16).

**2. Why his role was pivotal.**
- He was the link between the tribal league and the monarchy; without him the change would have lacked religious approval.
- He set the principle that the king is under God's word and subject to the prophet. This shaped the later relation of kings and prophets, as with Nathan and David.
- He kept the community faithful to the covenant during a time of transition.

**3. Limits.** The people started the request, and God agreed. Samuel acted reluctantly and under direction. Saul's rule ended in failure, and the success of the monarchy came through David, whom Samuel anointed but did not see on the throne.

**Conclusion.** Samuel was truly pivotal: he was the God-appointed agent who made and unmade kings and defined the relation between throne and covenant. Yet he remained a servant carrying out God's decisions.
